lessons.title: View Identity & the Render Loop
lessons.body:
SwiftUI views are **value types** — plain structs. Every time your state changes, SwiftUI calls `body` again and produces a fresh struct. It then **diffs the view tree** against the previous one to decide what actually needs updating on screen.

This diff relies on **identity**. SwiftUI uses two kinds:

- **Structural identity** — the view's type and position in the hierarchy. Most views get this automatically.
- **Explicit identity** — assigned with the `.id()` modifier. Use this to tell SwiftUI "this is a new view" even if it appears in the same position.

A view's **lifetime** is tied to its identity. As long as identity is stable, SwiftUI keeps the view alive and preserves its `@State`. The moment identity changes, SwiftUI destroys the old view and creates a fresh one — **all local state resets**.

This is why `ForEach` requires a stable `id` parameter. If ids change (e.g., using array indices on a mutable list), SwiftUI may destroy and recreate views unnecessarily, causing flickering and lost state.

```swift
// Stable string ids — state survives reorders
ForEach(items, id: \.id) { item in
    ItemRow(item: item)
}
```

Prefer `Identifiable` conformance or a stable, unique property as the id. Avoid using array indices when the array can be reordered or filtered.

quickCheck.prompt: What happens to a view's state when its identity changes?
quickCheck.explanation: Identity is the key SwiftUI uses to find existing state storage. A new identity means SwiftUI treats it as a brand-new view — no state is carried over.

options.text: State is migrated automatically to the new identity
It is destroyed and recreated from scratch
State is preserved across identity changes
A runtime error is thrown

lessons.title: State Management — @State, @Binding, @Observable, @Environment

quickCheck.explanation: @Binding is a derived reference — it points into a parent's @State storage. The child can read and write, but the parent owns the value and its lifetime.

options.text: An independent copy of the value, disconnected from the parent
A persistent storage entry owned by the child view
A two-way reference to a parent's @State
A strong reference to an ObservableObject instance

lessons.title: Layout System — Stacks, Frames, GeometryReader
lessons.body:
SwiftUI's layout follows a clear protocol: **parent offers size, child chooses its own size, parent places it**. Understanding this removes most layout mysteries.

**The three stacks:**
- `HStack` — horizontal axis
- `VStack` — vertical axis
- `ZStack` — z-axis (front to back layering)

**`.frame()`** lets you propose a specific size to a child or constrain it. `minWidth/maxWidth` create flexible ranges.

**`Spacer`** expands to fill available space along the stack's axis, pushing siblings apart.

**`layoutPriority`** controls which views shrink last when space is tight. Higher priority = last to compress (default is 0).

```swift
VStack {
    Text("Header")
        .frame(maxWidth: .infinity, alignment: .leading)
    Spacer()
    HStack {
        Text("Left").layoutPriority(1)
        Text("Right side with more content")
    }
    .padding()
    .frame(height: 44)
}
```

**`GeometryReader`** gives you the parent's offered size at render time. It's powerful but has a cost: it expands to fill all available space and can cause unexpected layouts. Use it only when you genuinely need dynamic sizing — not as a default wrapper.

Common pitfall: wrapping a simple view in `GeometryReader` just to get the screen width. Prefer `.frame(maxWidth: .infinity)` or environment values instead.

quickCheck.prompt: Which stack layers views along the z-axis (front to back)?
quickCheck.explanation: ZStack places its children on top of one another along the z-axis. The last child in the closure appears on top visually.

options.text: HStack
VStack
LazyVStack
ZStack

lessons.title: Navigation, Animation & Performance

quickCheck.prompt: A view's `.task { }` closure is still awaiting a network response when the view is removed from the hierarchy. What happens to that task?
quickCheck.explanation: `.task` ties the started work's lifetime to the view's identity — when the view disappears, SwiftUI cancels the task rather than letting it keep running unsupervised.

options.text: It's cancelled automatically — .task's lifetime is tied to view identity
It keeps executing independently of the view until the network call eventually completes
It pauses and resumes automatically once the view is shown again
It throws immediately, crashing the call stack unless wrapped in a do/catch

questions.prompt: What triggers SwiftUI to schedule a fresh evaluation of a view's `body`?
questions.explanation: SwiftUI records exactly which @State, @Binding, @Observable, or @Environment values body read on the last pass. Only a change to one of those specific values schedules a new evaluation — everything else is invisible to the diffing system.

options.text: Any stored property changing anywhere in the view, whether body reads it or not
A parent view re-rendering, even if this view's own state is untouched
A change to one of the dependencies body actually read on the previous pass
The app's scene phase moving from inactive to active

questions.prompt: How do @State and @Binding differ in who owns the value?
questions.explanation: @State is the source of truth — the view that declares it owns the storage. @Binding is a reference into someone else's storage; the view holding it can read and write but doesn't own the lifetime.

options.text: @State owns the storage; @Binding is a reference into it
@Binding owns the storage; @State merely observes changes to it
Both wrappers own independent copies of the value with no connection between them
@State only works with classes; @Binding only works with structs

questions.prompt: What's the practical difference between the @Observable macro and conforming to ObservableObject with @Published properties?
questions.explanation: @Observable tracks field access per-property automatically; a view only re-renders for the specific properties its body actually reads. ObservableObject publishes a single combined signal whenever any @Published property changes, so every observing view re-evaluates regardless of which property it reads.

options.text: ObservableObject is newer and supersedes @Observable for all use cases
@Observable requires manually calling objectWillChange.send() before every single mutation you make to a tracked property
ObservableObject already limits re-renders to only the views reading a changed property, no different from @Observable
@Observable re-renders only views reading the changed property; ObservableObject re-renders every observer

questions.prompt: SwiftUI views are declared as structs, recreated on every render. How does @State survive that?
questions.explanation: The struct instance itself really is thrown away and rebuilt each render. @State's actual storage lives outside the struct, in memory SwiftUI manages and keys to the view's identity — the fresh struct just points back at the same storage.

options.text: It doesn't — every render starts @State back at its initial value
SwiftUI keeps the storage outside the struct, keyed to identity; the new struct reattaches to it
The struct is only recreated the very first time it appears; every render after that mutates the original data in place
@State works by converting the view into a class at compile time

questions.prompt: What does tapping this button do, repeatedly?
questions.explanation: @State gives count persistent storage across renders. Each tap mutates it, SwiftUI notices body read count, and re-evaluates body — so the label updates to reflect the new value every time.

options.text: Nothing changes on screen after the first tap
It crashes at runtime because count is mutated from inside a button's closure
The label updates to show the new count after every tap
It compiles, but the label keeps showing Count: 0 no matter how many taps happen

questions.prompt: When does `.onAppear` fire on a view?
questions.explanation: .onAppear runs once, the moment the view is inserted into the visible hierarchy — not every time body re-evaluates. Its counterpart .onDisappear fires when the view leaves that hierarchy.

options.text: The moment the view is inserted into the visible hierarchy
Every time the view's body is re-evaluated
Only once a full second has elapsed since the view was created
When the view struct's initializer first runs, before layout

questions.prompt: Given this HStack, which Text keeps its ideal width first if space runs short?
questions.explanation: layoutPriority ranks views for compression order — SwiftUI shrinks the lowest-priority views first. Text A's explicit priority of 1 outranks Text B's default of 0, so B compresses or truncates before A gives up any space.

options.text: Text B, since it has more characters and needs more room
Neither — HStack splits its available space evenly between children regardless of layoutPriority
It's undefined and varies between runs
Text A, because its explicit layoutPriority(1) outranks B's default priority of 0

questions.prompt: What's the relationship between @Environment and @State?
questions.explanation: @Environment reads a value an ancestor placed into the hierarchy via .environment(_:_:) — it's inherited, not owned locally. @State is private, view-local storage the view itself owns and controls.

options.text: @Environment only works with primitive value types like Int and String; @State can hold reference types like classes too
@Environment values must be classes conforming to ObservableObject, while @State can hold any type
@Environment reads a value supplied by an ancestor; @State is storage the view owns itself
@Environment overrides whatever @State holds for that view

questions.prompt: A function returns `some View`. What does that return type actually mean?
questions.explanation: `some View` is an opaque type: the compiler knows and enforces one concrete, consistent type across every return path, but hides its name from callers. That's different from AnyView, which erases the type and allows switching between different concrete types.

options.text: One specific concrete type the compiler infers and hides the name of
Any type conforming to View, decided freshly at each call
A type-erased box, similar to AnyView, that can hold a different concrete view type on every single call
Functionally equivalent to declaring the return type as AnyView

questions.prompt: What's the practical difference between @StateObject and @ObservedObject?
questions.explanation: @StateObject creates and owns the object — SwiftUI keeps it alive across re-renders, tied to the view's identity. @ObservedObject just subscribes to an object that already exists and is owned somewhere else.

options.text: @StateObject and @ObservedObject are drop-in replacements for one another
@StateObject creates and owns the object across renders; @ObservedObject subscribes to one owned elsewhere
@ObservedObject is responsible for creating the object itself; @StateObject only subscribes to changes on it
@StateObject is meant only for value types like structs; @ObservedObject is meant only for reference types like classes

questions.prompt: A `ForEach` iterates over an array using `id: \.self` where elements are simple integers that can repeat. What's the risk?
questions.explanation: SwiftUI uses the id to match old and new elements when diffing. Duplicate ids mean two or more rows share an identity — SwiftUI can't tell them apart, so it may reuse the wrong row's state or misattribute animations between them.

options.text: Nothing — SwiftUI falls back to array position whenever two elements share an id
Compile error — the id: \.self parameter is only accepted for element types that already conform to Identifiable
ForEach only requires unique ids once the array's element count grows past roughly a hundred entries
Duplicate ids give two rows the same identity, so SwiftUI can misattribute state or animations between them

questions.prompt: Why is it cheap for SwiftUI to call a view's `body` and get back a brand-new struct on every state change?
questions.explanation: body is just a computed property returning a lightweight value-type description of the UI — no windows, layers, or rendering happen when it runs. SwiftUI diffs that description against the previous one and only touches the real render tree where something actually changed.

options.text: Because body only runs once per app launch and is cached afterward
Because body just returns a lightweight value-type description; nothing expensive renders until SwiftUI diffs it
Because SwiftUI recompiles and re-optimizes the view's source code on every single render pass triggered by a state update anywhere in the hierarchy
Because struct initializers in Swift are guaranteed not to allocate any memory

questions.prompt: This custom container takes `@ViewBuilder content: () -> Content`. What lets the call site use an `if/else` inside the trailing closure?
questions.explanation: @ViewBuilder is a result builder: it transforms an if/else inside the closure into a single value of a conditional wrapper type that itself conforms to View, so the trailing closure can still produce one Content value even though its branches return different concrete view types.

options.text: Content is declared using the type-erased `any View` existential, so any branch's concrete return type is accepted without restriction
The compiler infers a shared superclass for Text and LockedBadge
@ViewBuilder is a result builder that wraps the branches into a single conditional view value
Content must be declared as an enum with a case for each branch

questions.prompt: What's the difference between wrapping a state mutation in `withAnimation { }` and attaching `.animation(_:value:)` to a view?
questions.explanation: withAnimation wraps a specific state change explicitly — every view invalidated by that change animates the transition. .animation(_:value:) is attached to one view and only animates when the specific value it watches changes, independent of how the mutation that triggered it was written.

options.text: withAnimation animates a change explicitly; .animation(_:value:) reacts implicitly to one watched value
Both only take effect when the state change happens inside a Task { }
.animation(_:value:) only takes effect for views placed inside a List or a ScrollView; withAnimation works anywhere in the hierarchy
withAnimation is deprecated in favor of .animation(_:value:) as of iOS 17

questions.prompt: label changes right after isOnline flips. Does the Text update animate too?
questions.explanation: .animation(_:value:) is scoped to the value passed in — here, isOnline. A separate change to label isn't watched by that modifier at all, so Text's update happens without any animation from this call.

options.text: Yes, because both properties are read from within this view's body
Yes, but only during whichever render pass happens to change both properties together
No, because @State changes only animate when withAnimation explicitly wraps them
No, because .animation(_:value:) here only watches isOnline, not label

questions.prompt: What's the main practical advantage `NavigationStack` has over the older `NavigationView`?
questions.explanation: NavigationStack can be driven by a NavigationPath (or a plain array) that a view model owns, so pushing, popping, or restoring a whole navigation history programmatically doesn't require juggling hidden NavigationLink activation state the way NavigationView often did.

options.text: NavigationStack removes the need for a navigation title entirely
NavigationStack can be driven by a path value, making programmatic push/pop and state restoration straightforward
NavigationStack only supports pushing a single additional destination; NavigationView could push an unlimited depth of destinations
NavigationStack renders faster because it skips the navigation bar

questions.prompt: A view model needs to programmatically jump three levels deep into navigation — say, from a push notification — without every intermediate screen's type being known up front. What enables that?
questions.explanation: NavigationPath type-erases its elements, so a view model can append any Hashable destination values it wants — including several at once — without needing to reference the concrete View types that will eventually render them. navigationDestination(for:) maps each type back to its view when the stack actually renders that entry.

options.text: Declaring every possible destination in the entire app as a case inside one large shared enum threaded through the environment at the root view
Wrapping every destination view in AnyView ahead of time
Appending type-erased Hashable values to a NavigationPath and letting navigationDestination(for:) resolve each one to a view
Using NavigationView's isActive bindings chained three levels deep

questions.prompt: model.bio changes elsewhere in the app. Does NameLabel re-render?
questions.explanation: @Observable tracks access per property: NameLabel's body only reads model.name, so only changes to name are registered as a dependency. A change to bio, which body never touches, doesn't invalidate this view at all.

options.text: No — NameLabel only reads model.name, and @Observable tracks dependencies per property
Yes — any mutation to any property on an @Observable object re-renders every view holding a reference to it
Only if NameLabel is also marked @Observable itself
It depends on whether ProfileModel conforms to Equatable

questions.prompt: How do these two modifier orderings differ visually?
questions.explanation: Each modifier wraps the view built so far, and later modifiers apply to that wrapped result. padding-then-background gives the padding a colored background too, since the blue is applied after the padding is added. background-then-padding colors only the original text's tight bounds, and the padding sits outside that color, uncolored.

options.text: Modifier order only matters for stacks, not for individual views like Text
The first colors the padded area too; the second colors only the text's own bounds, leaving the padding uncolored
The first drops the background entirely, since a padded view can't accept a background afterward
The second effectively adds padding twice, because background implicitly re-applies the padding that came before it in the chain

questions.prompt: What must a custom type conforming to `Shape` implement to draw arbitrary vector graphics?
questions.explanation: Shape refines View but requires a single method — path(in:) — that returns a Path describing the outline to draw for a given CGRect. SwiftUI calls it with the frame it assigns and fills or strokes whatever Path comes back.

options.text: A draw(in:) method that renders pixels directly into a CGContext
A body property, exactly like any other ordinary View conformance, with no additional requirements to satisfy
An intrinsicContentSize property describing the shape's natural size
A path(in:) method that returns a Path describing the outline for a given rectangle

questions.prompt: A view wraps a single Text in GeometryReader just to read the screen width. What's the downside?
questions.explanation: GeometryReader expands to fill all the space its parent offers, regardless of what its content actually needs — so wrapping a simple view in it can quietly change that view's alignment and layout, not just hand back a size.

options.text: Nothing at all — GeometryReader has no effect on the surrounding layout unless you explicitly read values off its geometry proxy somewhere
It only works inside a List, so the Text disappears outside one
GeometryReader expands to fill all offered space, which can change the Text's layout and alignment unexpectedly
It forces the Text to render at a fixed 44-point height in every case

questions.prompt: A view three levels down reads `@Environment(\.brandAccent)` but no ancestor ever calls `.environment(\.brandAccent, _:)`. What color does it get?
questions.explanation: Every EnvironmentKey supplies a defaultValue, used whenever nothing further up the hierarchy has overridden it. Here that's .blue, so the view reads .blue rather than crashing or receiving an empty value.

options.text: .blue, the defaultValue declared on AccentKey, since nothing overrode it
A runtime crash at launch, since no ancestor view ever supplied a value for that particular key
Color.clear, SwiftUI's fallback for any unset environment key
Whatever value brandAccent held the very last time the app launched

questions.prompt: What does an `@FocusState` property let a view do that plain `@State` can't?
questions.explanation: @FocusState is a specialized property wrapper for text input and other focusable controls: binding it to a field's .focused($binding) modifier lets the view read and programmatically set which field currently has keyboard focus.

options.text: Store any Equatable value more efficiently than @State does
Read and programmatically set which focusable field currently has keyboard focus
Persist its value across app relaunches automatically
Share its current value across multiple completely unrelated views without needing any binding between them

questions.prompt: A view attaches `.task { await loadFeed() }`. The view disappears while loadFeed's network call is still in flight. What happens to that task?
questions.explanation: .task's lifetime is tied to the view's identity: when the view leaves the hierarchy, SwiftUI cancels the task it started automatically. loadFeed doesn't keep running unsupervised — it must check for cancellation itself if it wants to stop promptly.

options.text: It keeps running to completion regardless of the view disappearing
It's paused, then picked back up again if the view happens to reappear before finishing
It restarts loadFeed from the beginning the next time the view appears, ignoring the earlier call
SwiftUI cancels it automatically, since .task's lifetime is tied to the view's identity

questions.prompt: A child view needs to report its measured height so an ancestor can size a background to match. Which mechanism fits?
questions.explanation: PreferenceKey is the SwiftUI mechanism built for child-to-parent communication: a child sets a value via .preference(key:value:), and an ancestor collects it with .onPreferenceChange(_:), the mirror image of @Environment's top-down flow.

options.text: @Environment, since it already flows values through the whole hierarchy
@Binding, passed down through every intermediate view in the chain
A PreferenceKey, set by the child and observed by the ancestor via onPreferenceChange
GeometryReader alone, read directly from the ancestor's own frame without needing any involvement from the child view at all

questions.prompt: Every keystroke in NameField re-renders ExpensiveChart too, even though it reads neither name nor bio. Why?
questions.explanation: ProfileScreen's own body re-evaluates whenever any @State it owns changes — name and bio both live at that scope. body re-running means every child listed there, including ExpensiveChart, gets rebuilt as part of that same pass, whether or not it actually reads the changed value.

options.text: ExpensiveChart secretly reads an @Environment value that changes alongside name
ProfileScreen's body re-evaluates on any @State change at that scope, rebuilding every child listed in it
SwiftUI groups every sibling under one shared VStack into a single re-render batch as a built-in performance optimization
NameField and ExpensiveChart are declared with one @State property shared between them by mistake

questions.prompt: A view's body computes `data.sorted { $0.priority > $1.priority }` directly inside the view, on every render. What's the concern?
questions.explanation: body can run many times per second during animations or unrelated state changes elsewhere in the same view. Redoing an expensive sort on every single one of those passes wastes work that could instead be done once, elsewhere, and simply read by body.

options.text: The sort re-runs on every render, including ones triggered by unrelated state, wasting repeated work
Array.sorted can only be called once per app launch
SwiftUI defers the sort until the next explicit state change occurs, skipping over any unrelated renders in between
SwiftUI automatically caches any expensive call made inside body
